description: Turn one outfit photo into AI lookbook photos of one complete look. Use them on the collection page or a launch ad, and check every layer against stock.
h1: AI Lookbook Photos for One Complete Outfit
lead: A flat lay makes a full outfit hard to picture on a person. Upload one complete look and get AI lookbook photos for the collection page.
steps_h2: Make Fashion Editorial Photos in 3 Steps
steps_lead: Upload the full outfit, name one location and one light, then download the photo for the collection page.

steps.d: Lay the full outfit in one well-lit frame, layers separated. Include the top, bottom, outer layer, and shoes if they are part of it.
Name one location and one kind of light for an editorial still. Repeat that choice across the drop when the set should feel connected.
Check each layer against your stock, then add price and links outside the image. Publish only frames that still match the pieces you can ship.

faq.q: What should the source photo include?
faq.a: Show every piece in the look, including top, bottom, outer layer and the shoes or featured accessory, laid out in one frame. If a layer is missing from the source photo, do not treat the frame as if that piece is there.

faq.q: How do I keep a collection looking connected?
faq.a: Reuse one location, one light and one crop across looks, and let each garment stay distinct. Open the set with the hero outfit.

faq.q: Can I show more than one outfit in a single image?
faq.a: Use one full look per image so the silhouette stays clear. Make a separate image for the next outfit.

faq.q: Do I need a photographer or models?
faq.a: No. Each lookbook photo is generated from an outfit photo you already have. The person is generated, not someone you booked and not a customer.

faq.q: How is this different from hiring a creator?
faq.a: A creator needs samples, a fee and time on the calendar. Here you upload one photo, pick a scene and pay the credits for that job.

faq.q: What does a lookbook photo cost?
faq.a: Each photo costs 24 credits, the cost is shown before you start, and a failed job returns those credits. The download has no watermark, and you can use it in your own ads, pages and posts.

faq.q: Can the same scene cover menswear and womenswear?
faq.a: Yes, as long as each outfit has its own source photo and you keep the crop and light steady. Check tailoring and lengths against the garments you sell.

faq.q: Can I use the frames in a launch?
faq.a: Yes. They fit a collection page, a carousel or a launch email after you add prices yourself. A launch that also needs motion is covered by [product launch video and photos](page:occ-product-launch).

reviews.h2: How Sellers Build a Collection Launch Lookbook
reviews.lead: Example ways a label builds the set, including menswear lookbook photos.

items.d: Example: a womenswear label opens the drop with one full outfit on a person, then repeats the same crop and light. Each outfit still gets its own source photo.
Example: a menswear shop keeps the jacket, shirt and trousers visible together so the silhouette reads as one outfit. The next outfit is a second image.
Example: one street or studio description is reused so the carousel feels connected. Colors are checked against stock before the set is scheduled.

items.t: Collection page, not a shoot day
items.d: Example: the gallery is built from outfit photos the shop already has. Nobody is booked for a location day, and the person in frame is generated.
Example: each carousel slide is one outfit. Price and product links are added outside the image after download.

items.t: Credits instead of a creator day
items.d: Example: the agency uploads the outfit, picks a scene and pays the credits for that photo. It does not send samples out for this frame.
Example: each colorway gets its own source photo and the same crop, so the set stays easy to compare.
Example: the photos go on the collection page and in a launch email. Prices are added outside the image.
Example: a reseller checks jacket length and trouser length against the pieces it can ship before the set is scheduled.
Example: when shoes belong to the outfit, they are in the source photo and in the frame. A missing layer is left out.
